title: Load Testing: Finding the Limit Before Your Users Do
intro: Capacity numbers are guesses until you test them. Load tests answer 'how much can this handle, and what breaks first?'. Run them against staging (or production with great care), with the teams involved told in advance. The target here is the staging checkout API.

steps.prompt: Run the k6 script checkout.js with 100 virtual users for 5 minutes.
steps.fake_output:
scenarios: (100.00%) 1 scenario, 100 max VUs, 5m30s max duration
     ✓ status is 200
     checks.........................: 99.87% ✓ 148210 ✗ 193
     http_req_duration..............: avg=182ms p(90)=310ms p(95)=420ms max=2.9s
     http_req_failed................: 0.13%
     http_reqs......................: 148403 494.6/s
   ✗ http_req_duration..............: p(95)<400
ERRO[0301] thresholds on metrics 'http_req_duration' have been crossed
steps.explanation: About 495 req/s, but p95 latency is 420ms, above the 400ms threshold, so k6 exits non-zero.
steps.why: Read the percentiles, never the average: the average (182ms) looks fine while 1 in 20 requests takes over 400ms. Thresholds in the script turn the test into a pass/fail gate that can run in CI before every release.

steps.prompt: Find the breaking point at a fixed request rate regardless of response time: attack http://staging.shop.internal/api/cart at 800 req/s for 60s with vegeta and report.
expected_commands: echo "GET http://staging.shop.internal/api/cart" | vegeta attack -rate=800/s -duration=60s | vegeta report
echo 'GET http://staging.shop.internal/api/cart' | vegeta attack -rate=800/s -duration=60s | vegeta report
steps.fake_output:
Requests      [total, rate, throughput]  48000, 800.02, 612.40
Latencies     [min, mean, 50, 90, 95, 99, max]  4ms, 1.9s, 380ms, 5.1s, 8.2s, 30s, 30s
Success       [ratio]  76.55%
Status Codes  [code:count]  200:36744  503:6012  0:5244
Error Set:
Get "http://staging.shop.internal/api/cart": context deadline exceeded
steps.explanation: At 800 req/s only about 612/s complete. 23% fail with 503s and timeouts.
steps.why: vegeta sends at a constant rate whether or not responses come back (an 'open' model, like real users), whereas k6 VUs wait for each response (a 'closed' model), which hides overload. Constant-rate tests show how the system really fails: queues grow and latency explodes.

steps.prompt: While the test runs, find the bottleneck: check CPU and memory of the pods in namespace shop-staging, sorted by CPU.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                        CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
cart-5c7d9f8b6-h2j4k        1980m        410Mi
cart-5c7d9f8b6-p9q1w        1975m        402Mi
postgres-0                  240m         1.9Gi
redis-0                     60m          90Mi
steps.explanation: The cart pods are pinned at their 2-CPU limit; the database is fine.
steps.why: A load test is only useful if you learn what saturated first: CPU limits, a connection pool, the database, a downstream rate limit. The fix depends entirely on which one it is. Here it's cart's CPU, so scale it out or make it cheaper per request.

steps.prompt: Get a histogram of latencies from the saved result file results.bin, with buckets at 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, and 1s.
steps.explanation: Over 21% of requests took more than a second: a bimodal shape, with fast requests and ones stuck in a queue.
steps.why: Histograms reveal shapes percentiles hide: two humps usually mean some requests hit a queue, cache miss, or retry path and others don't. That's where to look next.
